locus.description: Bright green fedora worn by the male figure, directly above his face and centered in the frame

findings.claim: The bright green hat on the male model reads in China as 戴绿帽子 — 'wearing a green hat', the idiom for a man whose partner is cheating on him.
findings.rationale: In Mandarin, 戴绿帽子 (wearing a green hat) is the standard idiom for being cuckolded, which is why green hats are effectively unsellable menswear in China and why the phrase is an instant comment-section joke. Here the hat is the single brightest element in an otherwise neutral camel-and-grey frame, worn by a smiling man facing the viewer, so it is the first thing a Chinese viewer reads. On digital display, where the image is screenshot and reposted, the campaign invites the 'green hat' caption rather than the autumn-outerwear message.

precedents.title: Dove chocolate Qixi gift-box video nicknamed '绿帽巧克力' (green hat chocolate)
precedents.summary: Chinese netizens nicknamed a Dove Qixi promo video 'green hat chocolate' because its storyline cast the product as a prop for cheating; the 'green hat' label is the reflexive Chinese shorthand for cuckoldry.
precedents.outcome: Mars China pulled the video, delisted the gift box and apologized on Weibo.

precedents.title: 戴绿帽子 — the Chinese 'green hat' idiom
precedents.summary: In Chinese usage, to 'wear a green hat' means one's spouse or partner is unfaithful; the association is strong enough that green hats and green-hat gifts are avoided for men in the Chinese market.

findings.fixDirective: Recolour the green fedora to a neutral tone that sits with the outfit — charcoal grey or a deeper brown than the camel coat — keeping its shape, size and position unchanged.

analysis.reviewNotes: Examined the wordmark "NORTHLINE", the headline "Dressed for the season.", the body copy, the product name, the digital-display channel and every visual element (camel trench, charcoal knit and trousers, hat, flat grey background, figure's rendering). No launch date was supplied, so calendar-timing could not be checked. The only live referent I found for China is the green hat on a male figure ("戴绿帽子" = being cuckolded); I considered and ruled out the camel/brown palette, the Western trench-and-fedora silhouette (read as generic menswear, not military or period-specific), the brand name (no problematic Mandarin homophone), and the copy, which carries no idiomatic second reading in Chinese.
